name: Northern Pastaza Quichua
confidence_why: Orr 1962 and 1991, Nuckolls, Stanley, Nielsen and Hopper 2016, Nuckolls and Swanson 2018 and Rice 2025 all put default stress on the penultimate syllable, differing only over which morphological classes (third-plural -naun, disyllabic ideophones, locative contractions, stress-neutral enclitics) carry the exceptions.

new_statements.quote: 2. Stress and juncture. Stress is nonpredictable and therefore phonemic. It most frequently occurs, however, on the penultimate syllable of the word. In a few word classes stress may occur on the ultimate syllable: for convenience, therefore, we write stress only in the latter instances. wasi 'house', nina 'fire', rimana 'to tell', wasíy 'in the house', cagríy 'in the field', rimaún 'he is talking', mikúun 'he is eating', siriín 'he is lying down'. Stress is accompanied by high pitch. [p. 63] ... When the vowel and consonant are dropped, the stress remains on the syllable which was stressed when the full morpheme was present. [p. 75]

new_statements.relation_note: Same default placement as the catalog's penultimate rule (penultimate stress); adds the final-stress word classes, the high-pitch cue, and the retention of stress under locative truncation. The author's framing ('nonpredictable and therefore phonemic') is a type-level claim that a purely fixed: penultimate syllable label does not capture, but her own examples confine the exceptions to identifiable morphological classes rather than free lexical contrast.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word by default; in a few word classes (the examples are locative -y forms like wasíy, cagríy and contracted progressive 3sg verbs like rimaún, mikúun, siriín) it falls on the final syllable. The author calls stress 'nonpredictable and therefore phonemic' because of those final-stress classes, but the classes are morphologically defined. Stress is realised with high pitch; when the locative morpheme -ybi is truncated to -y the stress stays where it was in the full form.
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress in 'a few word classes' (locative -y forms, contracted progressive verbs); stress is marked orthographically only in those cases. Section 9 (pp. 75-77) compares eight Ecuadorian dialects but lists only segmental differences, none on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Orr 1962 is explicitly based on 'the Quichua of Puyo Pongo in eastern Ecuador' (p. 60), i.e. dialect H, Puyo Pongo, Pastaza province (p. 76), with a comparative section on seven other Ecuadorian Quichua dialects (Agato, Calderón, Salasaca, Colta, Cuenca, Saraguro, Dos Ríos/Napo) that lists only segmental differences. Orr 1991 is a pedagogical course in 'quichua de Pastaza', catalogued by the Rosetta Project under ISO qvz (Northern Pastaza Quichua). Both match the catalog item nort2973.

new_statements.quote: 1. Siempre que no este indicado, el acento cae en la penultima silaba de cada palabra. [Lección 1, Pronunciación] ... La palabra interrogativa es esdrujula; es decir, el acento cae en la antepenultima silaba. [Lección 4, on maitata 'a dónde'] ... En una conversacion o narrativa la particula ga que indica cambio de tema (leccion 2), generalmente no influye la posicion del acento en una palabra. Por lo tanto, el acento cae en la primera silaba de la palabra yaya-ga, como si yaya no llevase ningun sufijo. [Lección 13, Gramática]
new_statements.translation: 1. Unless otherwise indicated, the stress falls on the penultimate syllable of every word. ... The interrogative word is proparoxytone; that is, the stress falls on the antepenultimate syllable. ... In conversation or narrative the particle ga, which marks a change of topic (lesson 2), generally does not affect the position of stress in a word. Therefore the stress falls on the first syllable of the word yaya-ga, as if yaya carried no suffix.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is on the penultimate syllable of every word unless marked otherwise. Marked cases in the lessons: the interrogative maitata (interrogative stem + -ta) is stressed on the antepenult, and the topic enclitic -ga is ignored for stress placement, so yáya-ga keeps the stress of the bare word yáya.
new_statements.exceptions: Interrogative words with the particle -ta are proparoxytone (antepenultimate); the topic particle -ga does not count for stress (stress stays on the penult of the host word).
new_statements.identity_note: Orr 1962 is explicitly based on 'the Quichua of Puyo Pongo in eastern Ecuador' (p. 60), i.e. dialect H, Puyo Pongo, Pastaza province (p. 76), with a comparative section on seven other Ecuadorian Quichua dialects (Agato, Calderón, Salasaca, Colta, Cuenca, Saraguro, Dos Ríos/Napo) that lists only segmental differences. Orr 1991 is a pedagogical course in 'quichua de Pastaza', catalogued by the Rosetta Project under ISO qvz (Northern Pastaza Quichua). Both match the catalog item nort2973.

readall_conflicts: No placement conflict: both of Orr's works give penultimate stress as the default. There is a framing difference: Orr 1962 (p. 63) states that stress is 'nonpredictable and therefore phonemic' because a few word classes (locative -y forms, contracted progressive verbs) carry final stress, whereas Orr 1991 presents penultimate stress as the rule 'siempre que no esté indicado' with marked exceptions (antepenultimate on -ta interrogatives, stress-neutral topic enclitic -ga). The exceptions in both works are morphologically defined rather than lexically free, so a penultimate-default reading with morphological exceptions is compatible with both; a reader who takes Orr 1962's 'phonemic' claim literally would label the system lexical (unpredictable) instead.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-dominant penultimate, not strict' rests on a one-line pronunciation note in a 1991 SIL language course, quoted correctly (verified verbatim in the now-downloaded Rosetta excerpt, Lesson 1 Pronunciación §1). No better class of source (reference grammar, phonology monograph, instrumental study) exists for this language, but two more authoritative descriptions do exist and were downloaded: Rice 2025 PhD (U Alberta) §2.2.4 'Stress' pp. 73-74 and Nuckolls, Stanley, Nielsen & Hopper 2016 IJAL 82:103-104, 109, 113. Both state penultimate stress as the norm with lexically/morphologically restricted exceptions (3PL -naun final; disyllabic ideophones final; lengthened vowels from elided suffix consonants attract stress; some enclitics such as =mi and topic -ga stress-neutral, yielding antepenultimate; interrogative words antepenultimate per Orr). sources.quote: 'In most Quechuan languages, stress typically falls on the penultimate syllable of polysyllabic words (Adelaar & Muysken 2004: 206). This is largely true of Northern Pastaza Kichwa; however, there are some exceptions.' tone.quote: Stress is nonpredictable and therefore phonemic. It most frequently occurs, however, on the penultimate syllable of the word. In a few word classes stress may occur on the ultimate syllable [...] Stress is accompanied by high pitch. There are three junctures in Quichua, one terminal, and two nonterminal. The terminal juncture, #, is accompanied by falling voice on the syllable immediately preceding the juncture and a higher pitch on the stressed syllable of the word preceding the terminal juncture. [...] (High pitch is 4, low pitch is 1).
